### 14.7 The trim problem: NamedTuple decisions, declared reads, named residuals
- V1 The aircraft author ships one value.
- V2 It says what the solver may vary, what those decisions make of the model, what to read back after each evaluation, and which equations the readings must satisfy.
- V3 That value is a `TrimProblem`.
- V4 This section gives its fields, then its decisions and parameters, its reads, its residuals and checks, the formulation it encodes and its recorded extensions.

#### The fields
- V5 The field set is normative and closed (D-118, D-262). [D-118, D-262] (bold)
- V6 It is closed because the lift (§14.9) is field-by-field. [§14.9]
- V7 `guess`, `lower` and `upper` are same-named all-`Float64` NamedTuples (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V8 `condition` is the function over decisions whose value is a condition (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state).
- V9 `reads` is the declared read set.
- V10 `residuals` is the residual function.
- V11 `tolerances` is an all-`Float64` NamedTuple, same-named as the residual function's return.
- V12 `checks` is the check function, and `check_tolerances` an all-`Float64` NamedTuple same-named as its return.
- V13 Both default to empty.
- V14 `tolerances` is carried in the problem because a relocated problem must carry its own convergence test.
- V15 `at` (the scoping combinator storing a path prefix beside a node) passes it through untouched (D-118). [D-118]
- V16 Worked, the cruise case of Flight.jl's Cessna 172 model (`c172.jl`) reduces to its three-equation core.
- V17 The real problem is the same shape with the full 7-variable search, and the θ-constraint elimination survives inside `trim_condition`, the worked problem's illustrative condition function.
- V18 [code block] cruise = TrimProblem(
- V19 The rest of the section takes what the author ships one piece at a time, against Flight.jl's `c172.jl`.

#### Decisions and parameters
- V20 Decision variables, initial guess and box bounds are plain, same-named, all-`Float64` NamedTuples.
- V21 FlightPhysics' decision-variable supertype, `AbstractTrimState{N}`, is dropped.
- V22 It is an alias of StaticArrays' `FieldVector{N, Float64}`.
- V23 Its only job was vectorization, and vectorization is the service's (D-069). [D-069]
- V24 The service packs and unpacks by field order, and that order is the `guess` NamedTuple's own.
- V25 This seam runs on the rule §9.5 states, "the names are the pairing, order carries no semantics" (D-151). [§9.5, D-151]
- V26 `lower` and `upper` are checked at setup for key-set equality with `guess` and for `Float64` fields.
- V27 They are then canonicalized to `guess`'s field order by the same type-level reorder (`NamedTuple{keys(guess)}(lower)`).
- V28 A permuted bound spelling is therefore a non-event, rather than `α`'s bound silently applied to `throttle`.
- V29 A key-set or field-type mismatch is `TrimProblemInvalid`.
- V30 Guess, bounds and the returned solution share one spelling, and `Base.merge(guess, (throttle = 0.3,))` is free warm-start tweaking.
- V31 An author who wants a documented `@kwdef` struct keeps it privately and converts.
- V32 `TrimParameters` is the struct in Flight.jl's `c172.jl` that holds a trim's targets and settings.
- V33 `TrimParameters` stays a plain user struct the framework never sees (D-069, D-118). [D-069, D-118] (bold)
- V34 The assignment is the pure `trim_condition(ac, params, d)` fragment-tree function (§14.2), applied per iteration by the compiled plan (§14.4). [§14.2, §14.4]

#### Reads
- V35 The read side is declared, then compiled (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V36 The spelling is `reads(name = get_state(path, leaf) | get_deriv(path, leaf) | get_output(path, leaf) | get_input(leaf) | get_face(leaf), ...)`, the service read set (§14.4, D-124). [§14.4, D-124]
- V37 Each `leaf` is a leaf address (the field name with dotted and bracketed steps below it).
- V38 `get_state` and `get_deriv` address a declared state field and its derivative (validated against `x_init`/`s_init`).
- V39 `get_output` addresses a declared output port (validated against `y_types`).
- V40 `get_input` and `get_face` address a root input face and an output face (validated against the faces of the level the read set is mounted at, the root's when unmounted) (D-277). [D-277]
- V41 The path selectors (the closed family of deferred reads resolving against a source) reach any port the structure has (§13.3, D-414). [§13.3, D-414]
- V42 As authoring guidance, an equilibrium equation meant to survive substitution at a generic seam reads a face (D-414, D-125). [D-414, D-125]
- V43 A trim evaluation needing a value a component computes without declaring it finds no selector for it (§14.4). [§14.4]
- V44 That is a signal that the component should export it.
- V45 A derivative wanted across a contract boundary takes the same remedy.
- V46 Publish it as an ordinary output port computed in `y_direct`.
- V47 That is the one-line binding of the fused idiom (§5.3), made contract. [§5.3]
- V48 By convention, then, `get_deriv` stays inside subtrees the problem's author owns (D-414). [D-414]
- V49 The compiled reader fills a stack-only NamedTuple per evaluation.
- V50 It is the gather twin (§14.4). [§14.4]

#### Residuals and checks
- V51 The user supplies a residual system, not a scalar cost (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V52 It is authored as a NamedTuple of named equations.
- V53 The residual function that returns it has this signature.
- V54 [code block] residuals(reads::NamedTuple, d::NamedTuple) → NamedTuple
- V55 What the solver varies is passed, and what is fixed per problem is closed over (D-118). [D-118] (bold)
- V56 The gathered reads and the decision NamedTuple arrive as arguments.
- V57 `d` is the one value that cannot be closed over.
- V58 `TrimParameters` stays behind the closure, exactly as `condition` already holds it, and the framework never sees it.
- V59 Being user-shaped, that record is also where any environment handles the condition math needs conventionally ride.
- V60 §8.2 gives the value-level constructor (the plain exported function building a field handle from the component and input values) that builds such a handle, and §14.1 the pre-sweep doctrine. [§8.2, §14.1]
- V61 The problem receives the environment, and never writes it (§14.9). [§14.9]
- V62 The returned NamedTuple's names are the equation names the report and the failure messages use (D-118). [D-118]
- V63 The service packs residuals and tolerances to the solver's vector by field order.
- V64 The order is `tolerances`' field order, the declared side again, canonical for the r-side.
- V65 Each residual return is reordered to it (`NamedTuple{keys(tolerances)}(r)`) before packing (D-151). [D-151]
- V66 An equation list spelled in a different order inside the lambda therefore pairs correctly and costs nothing.
- V67 The decisions rule holds symmetrically on both ends of the seam.
- V68 Names pair, and order never does.
- V69 Names and types are checked at setup, because the guess evaluation the service performs anyway observes the residual key set.
- V70 A `tolerances` key-set mismatch, or any field-type disagreement on either side of the seam, is `TrimProblemInvalid` (Appendix C), with the offending field and the names or types in hand. [Appendix C]
- V71 Order is never a mismatch.
- V72 Checks are equations the service reports once, at the committed state, and never solves (D-262). [D-262] (bold)
- V73 `checks` has the residual function's signature, and `check_tolerances` pairs with its return as `tolerances` pairs with the residuals'.
- V74 The service gathers the checks after the commit, from the sweep of boundary zero (the initialization boundary, the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate), and reports them (§14.8). [§14.8]
- V75 Setup observes their return's shape at the guess evaluation, as it observes the residuals' (§14.8). [§14.8]
- V76 Their reads join the problem's one read set.
- V77 The reason for the checks lies in analytic elimination.
- V78 Under it, the condition math pins the airspeed and the flight-path angle from the targets and the atmosphere the user's `params` record holds, while the world measures against the atmosphere the baseline wrote.
- V79 If the two disagree, the residuals vanish at a true equilibrium that is not the requested point, and nothing in the residual system can tell (D-139). [D-139]
- V80 A check reading EAS (equivalent airspeed) from the world's airdata at the committed state and subtracting the requested value is where a world measurement meets the request, so any mismatch moves it.
- V81 The checks stay out of the solve because they carry no information for it (D-262). [D-262]

#### The formulation
- V82 The FlightPhysics formulation's core is correct and survives verbatim as user math (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V83 That core is analytic elimination, namely FlightPhysics' `θ_constraint` substituting the pitch constraint, filter and actuator equilibria imposed by construction, and the minimal 7-variable search.
- V84 What changes is the numerics.
- V85 Trim is a square root-find.
- V86 The Cessna 172 model's derivative-free scalar minimization over $\|r\|^2$ against a hand-scaled absolute `stopval` was the rational choice only because Jacobians through FlightCore's mutating `f_ode!` chain and the assignment math were out of reach (D-069). [D-069]
- V87 The default is nonlinear least squares on $r(d)$ with exact AD Jacobians, in the trust-region/Levenberg–Marquardt family (§14.8, D-069). [§14.8, D-069]
- V88 The `Dual` activation (the build's typed products at a given scalar type) seeds the decision variables through the `T`-generic assignment, sweep and `x_deriv`.
- V89 The seeds survive the condition write because a decision-descended leaf is `Dual`-typed in the shape and keeps its partials (§14.3, D-148). [§14.3, D-148]
- V90 Convergence is quadratic (~5–15 evaluations), the tolerances are per-residual and physical, and failure reports name the unbalanced equations with magnitudes.
- V91 The convergence verdict itself is service-owned and backend-independent (§14.8). [§14.8]
- V92 Non-squareness degrades gracefully (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V93 Redundant actuation becomes weighted or minimum-norm least squares.
- V94 Infeasible demands converge to a nonzero residual identifying the impossible balance.
- V95 At the solution, $\partial r / \partial d$ is free flight-physics data (control effectiveness) that cross-checks linearization.
- V96 The derivative-free scalar path would survive as the fallback, with Flight.jl's algorithm as its degenerate case (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V97 §14.8 gives the normalization of the residuals against the tolerances that would repair the hand-scaled absolute threshold. [§14.8]

#### Recorded extensions
- V98 Two problems are recorded, not built (a worked-out extension deliberately left unimplemented, its seams named) (D-069). [D-069] (bold)
- V99 They are closed-loop sampled-data trim and on-ground static equilibrium, each simply another problem value over the same service.
- V100 Closed-loop trim appends `s_update(s) - s = 0` residuals via a nondestructive scratch evaluation of `s_update`, which was structurally impossible under FlightCore's mutating `f_periodic!`.
- V101 On-ground static equilibrium solves strut compressions and attitude against gear forces.

### 14.8 The trim service: solver seam, scratch stores, commit and report
- V102 A `TrimProblem` is an inert value until a service runs it.
- V103 `trim!` is that service.
- V104 It drives a solver it holds behind one method, works on its own scratch stores (mutable working storage whose contents are never authoritative), commits a converged solution the way `init!` would, and returns a report.

#### The backend seam
- V105 The signature is `trim!(model, problem; baseline, t0 = 0.0, backend = LevenbergMarquardt())`, where `model` is a `Model` (a deployment materialized at one scalar type) at `Float64` (D-319). [D-319]
- V106 A `Model` at another scalar is refused as `ArgumentInvalid` with reason `:non_nominal` (D-319). [D-319]
- V107 A model that a simulation has claimed is refused before any check, as `ArgumentInvalid` with reason `:claimed`, since the call commits (D-319). [D-319]
- V108 The `baseline` keyword takes a baseline (an aircraft-shipped, full-coverage condition function).
- V109 `trim!(sim, problem; …)` gates on the simulation's lifecycle and commits through the simulation's `init!`.
- V110 The default backend is an in-house dense Levenberg–Marquardt (D-070). [D-070] (bold)
- V111 For decision dimensions ~10 with exact Jacobians, the core is ~100 lines, namely a damping loop, a small linear solve and a convergence test.
- V112 That is the §10.2 stepper precedent exactly, a tiny needed core against a heavy dependency. [§10.2]
- V113 The per-residual physical tolerances sharpen the case (§14.7). [§14.7]
- V114 They are a convergence test no external package spells natively.
- V115 That is precisely why the service, not the backend, applies it.
- V116 The backend seam is a pinned signature, value-passed, with one required method per backend (D-158). [D-158] (bold)
- V117 That one method is the seam.
- V118 [code block] solve(backend, eval!, d0, lower, upper, tol) -> (; d, status, n_evaluations, n_iterations)
- V119 `eval!(r, J, d)` is in-place and always fills `r`, the residual vector packed in `tolerances`' field order.
- V120 It fills `J` iff `J !== nothing`.
- V121 The Jacobian is requested by argument, so a Jacobian-free backend simply always passes `nothing`, and there is still exactly one evaluation method to implement.
- V122 `d0`, `lower` and `upper` are packed `Vector{Float64}` in `guess`'s field order, with `±Inf` meaning unbounded.
- V123 The declared side is canonical on both ends, and the service has canonicalized before packing (§14.7). [§14.7]
- V124 A backend that ignores bounds therefore ignores two vectors, not a missing argument.
- V125 `tol` is a `Vector{Float64}` in `tolerances`' field order.
- V126 It is data the backend may stop on, under the service's per-backend-family translation below, and it is decisive of nothing.
- V127 The return holds `d`, the solution, `status::Symbol`, and the diagnostic counts `n_evaluations` and `n_iterations`.
- V128 The status set is deliberately open, and the status is recorded verbatim in the report because the verdict is the service's (D-158). [D-158] (bold)
- V129 The name `solve` is subject to the exported-name audit (`pending.md`) like every other API spelling.
- V130 The backend sees vectors and never names, so the solution it returns unpacks by the same order it was given (D-151). [D-151]

#### The convergence verdict
- V131 The convergence verdict is the service's, uniformly (D-150). [D-150] (bold)
- V132 `converged` means `all(abs.(rᵢ) .≤ tolᵢ)`.
- V133 That is the per-residual box test (§14.7) in its own physical units, evaluated by the service at the backend's returned point. [§14.7]
- V134 It is one residual evaluation, noise against the solve that produced it.
- V135 That verdict, and nothing else, gates the commit and fills `TrimReport.converged`.
- V136 The backend's returned `status` is recorded in the report as diagnostic data, and it is authoritative over nothing.

#### The tolerance translation
- V137 The tolerance translation is the service's too, per backend family (D-150). [D-150]
- V138 In least-squares backends the tolerances are the stopping criterion.
- V139 They feed the per-residual test directly, so LM's damping loop tests exactly what the service will re-test.
- V140 The derivative-free fallback is designed and not yet built, and `pending.md` lists it (D-070). [D-070]
- V141 In the design it is `NLoptBackend(:LN_BOBYQA)` in a package extension.
- V142 It would pass `nothing` for the Jacobian, keep Flight.jl's algorithm one keyword away, and leave the framework core carrying zero optimizer dependencies.
- V143 For that fallback the service would square and normalize.
- V144 The objective minimized would be $\sum_i (r_i/\mathit{tol}_i)^2$ with `stopval = 1`.
- V145 That objective is dimensionless where the threshold in Flight.jl's Cessna 172 model (`c172.jl`) was hand-scaled and absolute (§14.7). [§14.7]
- V146 It is a well-scaled valley where a raw $\|r\|^2$ sums forces against moments.
- V147 The two criteria cannot disagree in the dangerous direction, because of this implication (D-150). [D-150]
- V148 $$\sum_i (r_i/\mathit{tol}_i)^2 \le 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (r_i/\mathit{tol}_i)^2 \le 1 \;\text{ for every } i$$
- V149 The `stopval` sphere is therefore inscribed in the tolerance box, and a fallback stopping at `stopval` necessarily passes the service's box test.
- V150 The converse disagreement, a backend stopping early and reporting an optimistic status, is caught by the re-check, which remains the single authority.
- V151 What is not claimed is point identity.
- V152 Different backends may land on different solutions, which is an algorithmic difference and a legitimate one.
- V153 What is eliminated is per-backend meanings of `converged`.

#### Box bounds and saturated decisions
- V154 Box bounds are honored by step projection (D-070). [D-070] (bold)
- V155 A decision variable saturated at the solution is listed in the report's saturated list, as `(:elevator, :upper)`.
- V156 That is the classic CG-limit diagnostic, which Flight.jl's trim leaves inferable only from mysterious residuals.

#### Scratch stores
- V157 Every `trim!` invocation instantiates a fresh working store set.
- V158 Each half of it (below) is a scratch `Model` of its own, materialized from the deployment the service was called on (D-317, D-319). [D-317, D-319]
- V159 The set holds the `x` backing, the `s` and `m` stores, the root input and signal tables, and the derivative buffer.
- V160 The set is built from the activation's layout (the build's typed products at a given scalar type).
- V161 The layout is the reusable compiled artifact.
- V162 The buffers are per-invocation and die with the call (stopped-sim allocation, §9.8). [§9.8]
- V163 Each set also calls every workspace (component-declared mutable scratch, arriving as `ws`) allocator once, at the activation's scalar (D-077). [D-077]
- V164 The `Dual` backend's buffers being un-aliasable by type is defense in depth, not the mechanism.
- V165 A `Float64` backend, such as the designed NLopt fallback, would get equally fresh buffers.
- V166 The invariant is backend-independent.
- V167 The simulation's authoritative stores have exactly one writer, the commit through boundary zero (the initialization boundary, the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate) (D-070). [D-070] (bold)
- V168 Setup applies `override(baseline, condition(guess))`, the problem's condition at the guess layered over the baseline by override, to the scratch set once.
- V169 That application's full coverage is checked here, as §14.6 requires (D-149). [§14.6, D-149]
- V170 Sweeps therefore see a complete world.
- V171 Raw instantiation is sound exactly because of that check, since every root input is written before any read.
- V172 An incomplete `baseline` is one declaration-ordered `UninitializedInputs` at setup rather than a whole solve against undefined cells.
- V173 The frozen cells are established, not probe-seeded (D-213). [D-213] (bold)
- V174 At the seeded activation the discrete tier is frozen (§9.4). [§9.4]
- V175 Its stages never run there, so nothing at that activation can derive a discrete output cell from the authored `s`.
- V176 Setup therefore instantiates the scratch set in two halves.
- V177 A nominal set (one at the `Float64` activation) takes the composite first, by the dynamic walk (§14.4), and runs one establishment round. [§14.4]
- V178 That round is boundary zero's sweep with every discrete output stage admitted, due or not (D-205), with no projection, no guards and no `s_update`. [D-205]
- V179 The seeded set is then written by the specialized `apply!`.
- V180 Its frozen cells are copied from the nominal set, `Float64` values that a continuous consumer reads as zero-partial constants (§9.5). [§9.5]
- V181 Every cell the iterations read is thus derived from the authored world.
- V182 A frozen cell holds what the authored discrete state publishes, which makes "held at the operating point" literal.
- V183 No scratch cell holds the probe's synthesized values.
- V184 That is the §14.6 barrier reaching the scratch world, as D-205 made it reach the published one. [§14.6, D-205]
- V185 The iterations are untouched.
- V186 They are raw write → sweep → read cycles at the seeded activation, over the continuous chain and `x_deriv` alone (§14.5). [§14.5]
- V187 The zero-decision problem (below) is the nominal half alone.
- V188 Its one evaluation is that establishment round, followed by one derivative evaluation for the reads (D-213). [D-213]
- V189 The commit applies the same composite over the same `baseline` (`override(baseline, condition(d))`, §14.9), so its coverage is setup's. [§14.9]
- V190 Commit's totality check is therefore structurally unfailable through the trim path, and it stands as the shared `init!` defense (D-149). [D-149]
- V191 A converged solve is always committable.
- V192 `TrimReport` therefore carries no committed flag, and the no-throw doctrine needs no exception.
- V193 Iterations rewrite the composite's write-set via the compiled plan.
- V194 The write-set is `override(baseline, condition(d))`, the same tree setup resolved, so a store both layers touch merges exactly as it did at setup.
- V195 An LM evaluation is one Dual-seeded sweep yielding `r` from the value parts and `J` from the partials, together (D-069). [D-069]
- V196 No convergence means no commit.
- V197 Non-convergence is the service's box test failing at the returned point, whatever status the backend attached to it (D-150). [D-150]
- V198 No commit means the sim is bit-for-bit untouched, including "never initialized".
- V199 Flight.jl's warn-but-assign is structurally impossible.
- V200 The same structure covers an interrupt.
- V201 Ctrl-C during a long solve unwinds an ordinary Julia call operating on per-invocation scratch stores.
- V202 No commit has happened, and the simulation is bit-for-bit untouched, exactly as a non-converged solve leaves it.
- V203 The services need no counterpart to the loop's boundary masking (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V204 An interrupt inside the commit's boundary zero moves the simulation to `built` and propagates raw (§13.4, D-223). [§13.4, D-223]
